title: KVCache metadata index rot: recovery playbook, compaction throttling, and load-shedding design
creator: Lena Park
summary: After a capacity surge on 2026-01-24 we observed a sustained memory growth in the KV prefix cache leading to eviction storms and service degradation in hosted inference. Investigation found a metadata index desynchronization between in-memory shard indices and concurrent background compaction that produced stale index entries ("rot"). The stale entries prevented proper reclamation of slab memory, caused slab fragmentation, and amplified eviction churn under load. This ticket captures the incident follow-up, short-term mitigations, and a durable remediation plan including compaction throttling, index reconciliation, and a safe load-shedding design.
impact: Peak latency spikes for text generation routes (p90 increased from 80ms to 560ms), sustained elevated OOM-like memory usage in the prefix cache pool, 18% request error rate increase for a 90-minute window, and several enterprise customers experienced request timeouts triggering support escalations.
timeline: 2026-01-24 02:10 UTC: An internal synthetic traffic spike correlated with model rollout. 2026-01-24 02:14 UTC: Observability alert -- prefix cache memory growth (heap and slab pools). 02:20 UTC: Autoscaling could not stabilize eviction; eviction storms observed. 02:50 UTC: On-call enabled aggressive eviction and disabled prefetch/predictive warming. 03:15 UTC: Temporary mitigation deployed: force-compaction + index sweep script; memory growth slowed. 04:00 UTC: Gradual recovery; post-incident analysis began.
detection_and_alerting: The incident was detected via the 'kvcache.slab_utilization' alert firing and client-side increased 5xx rates reported by Sentry. Existing dashboards showed a mismatch between 'active_entry_count' and 'free_slab_bytes' but no automated reconciler had run since compaction changes in runtime-1.22. Alert thresholds are being revisited to detect index skew earlier.
root_cause: Concurrent background compaction implemented in runtime-1.22 introduced a fast-path where index pointers were lazily updated. Under sustained allocation churn the lazy update path failed to atomically reconcile in-memory index buckets with compacted slab layouts. This produced stale index entries that referenced freed slab slots; the allocator's heuristics skipped reclamation for flagged entries, leading to fragmentation and apparent memory leakage. Eviction heuristics then over-prioritized recently-seen prefixes, causing eviction storms and request thrash.
immediate_mitigation: 1) Disabled lazy-index fast-path and reverted to conservative synchronous index updates. 2) Deployed an emergency force-compaction and index-sweep job across affected shards. 3) Temporarily disabled prefetch and predictive warming to reduce allocation pressure. 4) Applied conservative eviction cooldown (increase hysteresis) to avoid oscillation. These reduced memory growth and stabilized latency within ~40 minutes.

safety_and_rollback_plan: All compaction or index update changes must be feature-flagged and include a slow rollout path (canary by shard). Add a circuit-breaker that disables the new fast-path if slab_utilization increases > 12% in a 5m window or if index-mismatch alerts fire. Rollbacks should be automated via orchestration scripts referenced in the runbook.
postmortem_notes: We underestimated interaction between compaction concurrency and the allocator's lazy heuristics. The change landed without an invariant test covering pointer stability across concurrent compaction + rehash workloads. The incident exposed gaps in our integration tests and alerting for index-level correctness. We will add fuzz tests that simulate high allocation churn with compaction enabled.
